questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The activity of a radioactive sample decreases to one third of its original activity $A_{o}$ in a period of 3 years.

What is the activity of the sample after another 3 years?
questions.stemText: The activity of a radioactive sample decreases to one third of its original activity Ao in a period of 3 years. What is the activity of the sample after another 3 years? A 0.11 $A_{o}$ B 0.17 $A_{o}$ C 0.33 $A_{o}$ D 0.67 $A_{o}$

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognise that equal time intervals multiply activity by the same factor.
questions.misconception: Treating exponential decay as linear

explanation.body: For radioactive decay, $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$. At three years, $A_0/3=A_0e^{-3\lambda}$, so $\lambda=\ln(1/3)/(-3)=0.36620\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. At six years, $A=A_0e^{-0.36620(6)}\approx0.11A_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the second three-year interval as one half-life.
perOption.C: Gives the activity after only three years.
perOption.D: Gives the fraction lost in the first three years.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Nucleus P decays in two stages to produce nucleus Q. Which decay sequence will result in the highest number of neutrons in nucleus Q? A a $\beta$-particle followed by a $\gamma$-ray B an $\alpha$-particle followed by a $\gamma$-ray C an $\alpha$-particle followed by a $\beta$-particle D a $\beta$-particle followed by another $\beta$-particle

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Nucleus P decays in two stages to produce nucleus Q. Which decay sequence will result in the highest number of neutrons in nucleus Q?

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Tracking the neutron number change for each decay type.
questions.misconception: Thinking β-decay leaves the neutron number unchanged or that γ emission changes the nucleus composition

explanation.body: Let R be the intermediate nucleus. Beta decay gives $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{P}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}+{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$, followed by gamma decay $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Q}+\gamma$. The neutron number in Q is $A-(Z+1)=A-Z-1$.

perOption.A: Correct. The neutron count drops by just one.
perOption.B: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and gamma emission leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.C: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and beta-minus decay converts one more into a proton.
perOption.D: Each beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so the count drops by two.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A radioactive source is placed near a detector and the reading is 324 counts per minute. After two half-lives, the reading drops to 108 counts per minute.

What is the background radiation in counts per minute?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source is placed near a detector and the reading is 324 counts per minute. After two half-lives, the reading drops to 108 counts per minute. What is the background radiation in counts per minute? A 27 B 36 C 54 D 72

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires separating the constant background from the decaying source count over two half-lives.
questions.misconception: Halving the total count rate, including background, each half-life

explanation.body: Let $C$ be the initial count rate due to the source alone. After two half-lives it has fallen by $3C/4$, so $3C/4=324-108$ and $C=288\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $324-288=36\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Quarters the later reading even though it includes a constant background contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. The background contributes 36 counts per minute.
perOption.C: Halves the later reading even though the half-life applies only to the source contribution.
perOption.D: Gives the remaining source count rate after two half-lives.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The figure shows part of a chart of nuclides where neutron number is plotted against proton number. An unstable nuclide X decays spontaneously by emitting a $\beta$-particle. Into which nuclide does it decay? [Grid: proton number 91–96 on x-axis, neutron number 140–147 on y-axis. Points: A at (92, 141), C at (93, 145), X at (94, 145), D at (95, 145), B at (95, 144).]

stemImage.alt: Question 29: The figure shows part of a chart of nuclides where neutron number is plotted against proton number. An unstable nuclide X decays spontaneously by emitting a 훽-p

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Applies $\beta^-$ decay changes to a nuclide chart.
questions.misconception: Swapping proton and neutron changes in beta decay

explanation.body: In $\beta^-$ decay, a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. The proton number rises from $94$ to $95$, and the neutron number falls from $145$ to $144$. This is one square right and one square down from X, at B.

perOption.A: Lowers both counts, whereas beta-minus decay raises the proton count by one and lowers the neutron count by one.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Lowers the proton count and leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.D: Raises the proton count correctly but leaves the neutron count unchanged.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: α-particles are observed to be deflected by a thin metal foil through angles that range from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$. Which of the following could explain this observation? A Due to diffraction from the crystal lattice in the metal. B Due to reflection from the surface of the foil. C Due to scattering from electrons in the metal. D Due to scattering from the small highly positive charged nuclei of atoms in the metal.

stemImage.alt: Question 30: -particles are observed to be deflected by a thin metal foil through angles that range from 0 to 180. Which of the following could explain this observation?

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the Rutherford scattering interpretation.
questions.misconception: Attributing large-angle scattering to electrons

explanation.body: The foil contains small, heavy, positively charged nuclei that repel the positively charged alpha particles. Close encounters can deflect an alpha particle by more than $90^\circ$, including nearly straight back. These large deflections are explained by scattering from individual nuclei in the foil.

perOption.A: Attributes the large-angle scattering to diffraction by the crystal lattice.
perOption.B: Treats the foil surface as a reflector and misses scattering by nuclei within the foil.
perOption.C: Electrons are too light to produce the observed large deflections of alpha particles.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A sample of a radioactive isotope with nucleon number 210 decays by alpha emission into a stable isotope with nucleon number 206. The process has a half-life of 140 days. If all the emitted alpha-particles escape from the sample but none of the daughter product escapes, what will be the percentage decrease in the mass of the source after 280 days?
questions.stemText: A sample of a radioactive isotope with nucleon number 210 decays by alpha emission into a stable isotope with nucleon number 206. The process has a half-life of 140 days. If all the emitted alpha-particles escape from the sample but none of the daughter product escapes, what will be the percentage decrease in the mass of the source after 280 days? A 0.48% B 1.43% C 25% D 75%

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Unfamiliar twist: mass lost is only the escaping alpha particles, not the decayed nuclei.
questions.misconception: Equating the mass lost with the fraction of nuclei decayed

explanation.body: Starting with $N$ nuclei, $3N/4$ decay in two half-lives. Approximating nuclear masses by their nucleon numbers in atomic mass units, the change is $\Delta m=[-(3N/4)(210)+(3N/4)(206)]\,\mathrm u=-3N\,\mathrm u$. Relative to the initial mass $210N\,\mathrm u$, this is a decrease of $1/70\approx1.43\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the surviving quarter of the parent nuclei to count the emitted alpha particles.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Confuses the fraction of parent nuclei remaining with the fraction of mass lost.
perOption.D: Assumes the full mass of each decayed nucleus leaves the sample.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: In medical radiotherapy, different types of radioactive emissions are chosen based on their penetrating abilities and ionising effects. Which combination correctly matches the emission type with its most appropriate medical application?
questions.stemText: In medical radiotherapy, different types of radioactive emissions are chosen based on their penetrating abilities and ionising effects. Which combination correctly matches the emission type with its most appropriate medical application? A alpha particles - external beam therapy for deep tumours B beta particles - treating shallow skin cancers and surface tumours C gamma rays - treating only surface-level conditions D alpha particles - medical imaging of internal organs

options.label: A
options.text: alpha particles - external beam therapy for deep tumours

options.label: B
options.text: beta particles - treating shallow skin cancers and surface tumours

options.label: C
options.text: gamma rays - treating only surface-level conditions

options.label: D
options.text: alpha particles - medical imaging of internal organs

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall of penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
questions.misconception: Mixing up the penetrating abilities of alpha, beta and gamma

explanation.body: Beta particles can penetrate several millimetres into tissue and deposit ionising energy in surface and near-surface tumours. Their limited range helps spare deeper healthy tissue.

perOption.A: Alpha particles are stopped by the outer layer of skin before reaching a deep tumour.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gamma rays can reach deep tissues, so their use is not limited to surface conditions.
perOption.D: Alpha particles emitted inside the body have too short a range to reach external detectors.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A radioactive source is placed 5 cm from a Geiger-tube, and the various absorbers are placed in between. For each absorber, a one-minute count is taken of the total number of decays, and this is repeated several times.

The table shows the results of the experiment. The background count was 300 per minute.

What nuclear radiation does this suggest the source was emitting?
questions.stemText: A radioactive source is placed 5 cm from a Geiger-tube, and the various absorbers are placed in between. For each absorber, a one-minute count is taken of the total number of decays, and this is repeated several times. The table shows the results of the experiment. The background count was 300 per minute. average number of decays absorber detected in one minute none 1044 0.1 mm paper 1038 0.1 mm aluminium 496 1 mm lead 301 What nuclear radiation does this suggest the source was emitting? A beta only B alpha and beta only C beta and gamma only D alpha, beta and gamma

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Read a data table against known penetrating powers, allowing for background.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to subtract background, so the 301 count with lead looks like gamma

explanation.body: Subtracting the background of 300 counts per minute gives net counts of 744, 738, 196 and 1 per minute for no absorber, paper, aluminium and lead respectively. Paper makes little difference, so the readings give no evidence of alpha radiation. The aluminium reduces the count by 542 per minute, consistent with beta absorption. With 1 mm of lead the count returns to approximately background, so the residual count through aluminium is consistent with more penetrating beta particles.

perOption.A: Correct. The absorption pattern suggests beta only.
perOption.B: The negligible change with paper gives no evidence of alpha radiation.
perOption.C: The count with lead is approximately background, so the measurements give no evidence of a detectable gamma component.
perOption.D: Paper and lead give no evidence of detectable alpha or gamma components.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Meteorites collected in Antarctica can be used to date the solar system by using the radioactive decay of rubidium-87 to strontium-87. The half-life for this decay is $4.88\times10^{10}$ years. In a particular meteorite the present ratio of strontium-87 to rubidium-87, after correcting for the presence of strontium when the meteorite formed, is 0.062. Assume that there was no strontium-87 when the meteorite was created, how old is the meteorite? A $3.03\times10^{9}$ years B $4.24\times10^{9}$ years C $4.51\times10^{9}$ years D $4.58\times10^{10}$ years

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Meteorites collected in Antarctica can be used to date the solar system by using the radioactive decay of rubidium-87 to strontium-87. The half-life for this de

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the ratio converted to $N_0/N$ before applying exponential decay with the half-life.
questions.misconception: Treating the daughter-to-parent ratio as the fraction decayed or as the fraction remaining

explanation.body: The present ratio is $N_{\mathrm{Sr}}/N_{\mathrm{Rb}}=0.062$. Since $N_{\mathrm{Sr}}=N_0-N_{\mathrm{Rb}}$, the surviving rubidium fraction is $N_{\mathrm{Rb}}/N_0=1/1.062\approx0.9416$. Using $N_{\mathrm{Rb}}/N_0=e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln2/t_{1/2}$ gives $t=-\frac{\ln(0.9416)}{\ln2}(4.88\times10^{10})\approx4.24\times10^9$ years.

perOption.A: This age is too short to produce the observed strontium-to-rubidium ratio.
perOption.B: Correct. The surviving fraction gives an age of about 4.24 billion years.
perOption.C: Treating 0.062 as the fraction of the initial rubidium that decayed gives an age close to this value.
perOption.D: This age is almost one half-life, which would give a daughter-to-parent ratio near one.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Which of the following statements concerning nuclear properties is true? A The greater the binding energy of a nucleus, the more stable it is. B If the total rest mass of the products of a reaction is greater than the total rest mass of the reactants, this reaction is impossible. C When a stationary nucleus decays by emitting a $\gamma$-photon, the nucleus will move off in an opposite direction to the photon. D The half-life of a radioactive substance can be changed by allowing the substance to react chemically to produce a new radioactive compound.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Which of the following statements concerning nuclear properties is true?

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Tests several subtle points: binding energy vs per nucleon, mass-energy in reactions, momentum conservation and decay independence.
questions.misconception: Judging nuclear stability by total binding energy rather than binding energy per nucleon

explanation.body: The total linear momentum is zero before the stationary nucleus emits the $\gamma$ photon. By conservation of linear momentum, the recoiling nucleus must have momentum equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the photon’s momentum.

perOption.A: Nuclear stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon rather than total binding energy.
perOption.B: A reaction with greater product rest mass can occur if enough energy is supplied to the reactants.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: In the usual nuclear-decay model, chemical reactions leave the half-life of the radionuclide unchanged.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A uranium-235 nucleus $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ undergoes fission, producing nuclei of lanthanum-146 $^{146}_{57}\mathrm{La}$ and bromine-87 $^{87}_{35}\mathrm{Br}$. The binding energies per nucleon of these nuclides are shown below. [Table: $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}$: 7.6 MeV; $^{146}_{57}\mathrm{La}$: 8.2 MeV; $^{87}_{35}\mathrm{Br}$: 8.6 MeV] What is the energy released during fission of uranium-235? A 9.2 MeV B 69.2 MeV C 90.2 MeV D 159.4 MeV

stemImage.alt: Question 30: 92U undergoes fission, producing nuclei of lanthanum-146 146 A uranium-235 nucleus 235 57La and bromine-87 87 35Br . The binding energies per nucleon of these n

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs total binding energies (BE per nucleon × A) and their difference, not a difference of per-nucleon values.
questions.misconception: Subtracting binding energies per nucleon instead of total binding energies

explanation.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactant. Multiplying each binding energy per nucleon by its nucleon number gives $(8.2\times146)+(8.6\times87)-(7.6\times235)=159.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Combines the tabulated per-nucleon values without weighting by nucleon number.
perOption.B: Undercounts the net binding-energy gain of the two fragments combined.
perOption.C: Undercounts the net binding-energy gain of the two fragments combined.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two $\alpha$-particles with equal energies are fired towards the nucleus of a gold atom. Which diagram could represent their paths? [A: two parallel paths above the nucleus both deflected upward away from it, the lower (closer) one more sharply. B: upper path undeflected, lower path deflected upward. C: both paths deflected upward by the same angle. D: both paths bend downward towards/around the nucleus.]

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Two 훼-particles with equal energies are fired towards the nucleus of a gold atom. Which diagram could represent their paths?

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires knowing that the closer alpha particle feels greater repulsion and is deflected more.
questions.misconception: Thinking alpha particles are attracted to the nucleus or that farther particles deflect more

explanation.body: The positively charged gold nucleus repels both alpha particles. Of the two particles with equal energies, the one passing closer to the nucleus is deflected through the larger angle.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows the farther particle continuing straight even though the nucleus also repels it.
perOption.C: Shows the same deflection for both particles despite their different distances from the nucleus.
perOption.D: Shows both particles bending towards the positively charged nucleus.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: For many unstable parent nuclei, the daughter product is itself radioactive. Initially only the parent isotope P is present. P decays into daughter $D_1$, which decays to form $D_2$. [Graph: number of nuclei against time/years from 0 to 60. P falls exponentially from its maximum, reaching half at about 3 years. $D_1$ rises to a peak at about 9 years then decays slowly. $D_2$ rises steadily towards the initial number.] Which correctly describes the half-lives of P and $D_1$? A 3 years, 20 years B 3 years, 15 years C 6 years, 20 years D 6 years, 15 years

stemImage.alt: Question 30: For many unstable parent nuclei, the daughter product is itself radioactive. Initially, only the parent isotope P is present in the sample. The parent isotope P

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must read P's half-life directly and find D1's half-life from its tail after P has decayed.
questions.misconception: Reading D1's half-life from its peak or from the start rather than its exponential tail

explanation.body: The number of parent nuclei halves from its initial value in about 3 years. To estimate the half-life of $D_1$, use the part of the curve where very little P remains, so production of new $D_1$ is negligible. The number of $D_1$ nuclei at year 29 is about halved by year 44, giving 15 years.

perOption.A: Uses a 20-year interval for the daughter, whose late-time count halves in about 15 years.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates both half-lives by reading intervals longer than the respective halving times.
perOption.D: Uses about 6 years for P, by which time its count has roughly quartered.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The ratio of $^{14}$C : $^{12}$C in living things is fixed when they are alive but decreases after death because of the radioactive decay of $^{14}$C. $^{14}$C has a half-life of 5730 years. A 10.0 g sample of wood cut from a live tree is measured to have an activity of 120 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$.

If a 1.0 g sample of an old wooden relic is found to have an activity of 8.05 $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$, how long ago was this wooden relic cut from a live tree?
questions.stemText: The ratio of 14C : 12C in living things is fixed when they are alive but decreases after death because of the radioactive decay of 14C. 14C has a half-life of 5730 years. A 10.0 g sample of wood cut from a live tree is measured to have an activity of 120 min−1. If a 1.0 g sample of an old wooden relic is found to have an activity of 8.05 min−1, how long ago was this wooden relic cut from a live tree? A 1470 years B 3300 years C 9950 years D 22300 years

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs normalising activity per gram before applying exponential decay.
questions.misconception: Comparing activities without scaling for sample mass

explanation.body: Activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei, so $1.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of live wood would have an activity of $120/10=12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Using $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/5730\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ gives $8.05=12.0e^{-(\ln 2)t/5730}$, with $t$ in years. Solving gives $t\approx3300$ years.

perOption.A: This age allows too little decay, leaving more than $8.05\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ from a $12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ starting activity.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass-adjusted activity ratio gives about 3300 years.
perOption.C: Uses an age beyond one half-life even though more than half the initial activity remains.
perOption.D: Compares the activities directly without adjusting for the tenfold difference in sample mass.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Uranium-235 undergoes fission in a reaction shown below, releasing 195 MeV of energy. The binding energy per nucleon for uranium-235 is 7.6 MeV. The binding energy per nucleon for caesium and rubidium are each approximately equal to X MeV. $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + ^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow ^{143}_{55}\mathrm{Cs} + ^{90}_{37}\mathrm{Rb} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$ What is the value of X? A 6.7 B 6.8 C 8.4 D 8.5

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Uranium-235 undergoes fission in a reaction shown below, releasing 195 MeV of energy. The binding energy per nucleon for uranium-235 is 7.6 MeV. The binding ene

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs energy release as the increase in total binding energy, counting nucleons correctly.
questions.misconception: Including free neutrons in the product binding energy

explanation.body: The energy released equals the products’ total binding energy minus the reactants’ total binding energy. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235(7.6)$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.50\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon.

perOption.A: Reverses the energy difference and also uses too many bound product nucleons.
perOption.B: Subtracts the released energy from the initial binding energy instead of adding it.
perOption.C: Averages over too many nucleons by counting free neutrons in the product binding-energy calculation.
perOption.D: Correct. The 195 MeV increase is shared across 233 bound product nucleons.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A radioactive sample consists of two nuclides.

One has a half-life of $48\ \mathrm{h}$ and decays by emitting alpha particles, while the other has a half-life of $36\ \mathrm{h}$ and emits beta particles.

The initial count rate is $352\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. When a sheet of paper is placed between the source and the detector, the count rate becomes $256\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $16\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

What will the count rate be after 6 days, without the paper present?

A. $27\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
B. $36\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
C. $43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$
D. $52\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A radioactive sample consists of two nuclides. One has a half-life of 48 h and decays by emitting alpha particles, while the other has a half-life of 36 h and e

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires isolating two source rates, decaying them separately and restoring the background.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to background counts

explanation.body:
Paper stops alpha particles, so the initial alpha count rate is $352-256=96\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and the initial beta count rate is $256-16=240\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Six days is $144\ \mathrm{h}$, or three alpha half-lives and four beta half-lives.

The final alpha and beta count rates are $96/2^3=12\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and $240/2^4=15\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Adding the background gives $12+15+16=43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Leaves out the background count at the detector.
perOption.B: Undercounts the source contribution, for example by applying too many half-lives.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overcounts the source contribution by allowing too little decay.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The following process shows a stationary isotope of boron, which upon capturing a slow-moving neutron, splits to form a lithium isotope and an alpha particle.

$\,^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}+\,^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\to\,^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}+\,^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}+\gamma$

The nuclear binding energies per nucleon of the isotopes are:

$\,^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}$: $6.494\ \mathrm{MeV}$
$\,^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$: $5.607\ \mathrm{MeV}$
$\,^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$: $7.120\ \mathrm{MeV}$

What is the energy of the $\gamma$-ray emitted, given that the total kinetic energy of $\,^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$ and $\,^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ is $2.31\ \mathrm{MeV}$?

A. $0.48\ \mathrm{MeV}$
B. $2.79\ \mathrm{MeV}$
C. $5.10\ \mathrm{MeV}$
D. $6.23\ \mathrm{MeV}$

stemImage.alt: Question 30: The following process shows a stationary isotope of boron, which upon capturing a slow-moving neutron, splits to form a lithium isotope and an alpha particle. +

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires calculating total binding energies and allocating the released energy to kinetic energy and the photon.
questions.misconception: Equating total released energy to photon energy

explanation.body: The energy released is the increase in total binding energy, $(5.607\times7+7.120\times4-6.494\times10)\ \mathrm{MeV}=2.789\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Subtracting the products' total kinetic energy gives a $\gamma$-ray energy of $2.789-2.31=0.479\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx0.48\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the total released energy without deducting the products' kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Adds the products' kinetic energy to the released energy.
perOption.D: Overstates the energy available from the change in binding energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In the $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment, a beam of $\alpha$-particles is aimed at a thin gold foil. Most of the $\alpha$-particles go straight through or are deflected by a small angle. A very small proportion are deflected through more than $90^\circ$, effectively rebounding towards the source of the $\alpha$-particles.

Which conclusion about the structure of atoms cannot be drawn from this experiment alone?

A  Most of the atom is empty space.
B  Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
C  The nucleus contains both protons and neutrons.
D  The nucleus is charged.

stemImage.alt: Question 29: In the 훼-particle scattering experiment, a beam of 훼-particles is aimed at a thin gold foil. Most of the 훼-particles go straight through or are deflected by a s

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Distinguish the inferences from scattering data from claims about nuclear composition.
questions.misconception: Inferring neutrons directly from Rutherford scattering

explanation.body: The scattering experiment reveals a small, massive, charged nucleus. The scattering observations do not reveal whether the nucleus contains neutrons, so they cannot establish that it contains both protons and neutrons.

perOption.A: Most alpha particles pass straight through or are only slightly deflected, which supports this inference.
perOption.B: The rare rebounds show that mass is concentrated in a small nucleus capable of deflecting an alpha particle through a large angle.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The deflections of the charged alpha particles show that they interact electrically with the nucleus.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
In a radioactive decay series, three successive decays each result in a particle being emitted.

The first decay results in the emission of a $\beta^-$ particle. The second decay results in the emission of an $\alpha$ particle. The third decay results in the emission of another $\beta^-$ particle.

[Decay diagram P → Q → R → S, with outgoing arrows labelled $\beta^-$ from P, $\alpha$ from Q and $\beta^-$ from R.]

Nuclides P and S are compared.

Which statement about S is correct?

A  S and P are identical in all respects.
B  S and P are isotopes of the same element.
C  S is a different element of a lower atomic number.
D  S is a different element of reduced mass.

stemImage.alt: Question 30: In a radioactive decay series, three successive decays each result in a particle being emitted. The first decay results in the emission of a β− particle. The se

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Track both proton and nucleon numbers across the three successive decays.
questions.misconception: Tracking the alpha decay without both beta decays

explanation.body: Each $\beta^-$ decay increases the proton number by one and leaves the mass number unchanged. The $\alpha$ decay decreases the proton number by two and the mass number by four. Thus S has the same proton number as P and four fewer nucleons, making them isotopes of the same element.

perOption.A: The alpha decay leaves S with four fewer nucleons than P.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This overlooks the two beta decays that cancel the alpha decay’s effect on proton number.
perOption.D: The mass number falls, but the unchanged proton number means S belongs to the same element.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A radioactive source consists of $64\times10^{12}$ atoms of nuclide P of half-life 2 days. Another source consists of $8\times10^{12}$ atoms of nuclide Q of half-life 3 days. After how long will the number of undecayed nuclei in the two sources be equal?

A 6 days
B 9 days
C 12 days
D 18 days

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A radioactive source consists of 64  1012 atoms of nuclide P of half-life 2 days. Another source consists of 8 x 1012 atoms of nuclide Q of half-life 3 days. A

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires equating two decay laws with different half-lives and simplifying the powers.
questions.misconception: Confusing elapsed time with the number of half-lives

explanation.body: Set the surviving populations equal using $N=N_0(1/2)^{t/t_{1/2}}$. Cancelling the common factor of $10^{12}$ gives $64(1/2)^{t/2}=8(1/2)^{t/3}$, with $t$ in days. Thus $(1/2)^{t/2-t/3}=2^{3-6}$, so $t/6=3$ and $t=18$ days.

perOption.A: Allows for a difference of only one half-life, leaving P with four times as many nuclei as Q.
perOption.B: Allows for a difference of only 1.5 half-lives, leaving more P nuclei than Q nuclei.
perOption.C: Allows for a difference of only two half-lives, leaving twice as many P nuclei as Q nuclei.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The binding energy per nucleon of iron-56 is 8.8 MeV.

What happens when an iron-56 nucleus is created from its constituent protons and neutrons?
questions.stemText: The binding energy per nucleon of iron-56 is 8.8 MeV. What happens when an iron-56 nucleus is created from its constituent protons and neutrons? A 8.8 MeV of energy is absorbed. B 8.8 MeV of energy is absorbed. C 8.8 MeV of energy is released. D 493 MeV of energy is absorbed. 493 MeV of energy is released.

options.label: D
options.text: 493 MeV of energy is absorbed. 493 MeV of energy is released.

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires scaling the binding energy per nucleon and identifying the direction of energy transfer.
questions.misconception: Confusing binding energy per nucleon with total binding energy

explanation.body: Iron-56 has 56 nucleons, so its total binding energy is $8.8\times56=492.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Forming the nucleus releases this energy, approximately $493\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Uses the energy per nucleon and reverses the direction of transfer.
perOption.B: Uses the energy per nucleon as the total.
perOption.C: Gives the energy needed to separate the nucleus into nucleons.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The equation

$^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}+{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\rightarrow{}^{121}_{45}\mathrm{Rh}+{}^{113}_{47}\mathrm{Ag}+2\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$

shows the fission of a uranium-235 nuclide by a slow-moving neutron into a rhodium-121 nuclide, a silver-113 nuclide and two neutrons.

binding energy per nucleon of $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}=7.59\ \mathrm{MeV}$
binding energy per nucleon of $^{121}_{45}\mathrm{Rh}=8.26\ \mathrm{MeV}$
binding energy per nucleon of $^{113}_{47}\mathrm{Ag}=8.52\ \mathrm{MeV}$

What is the energy released during this fission process?

A $9.19\ \mathrm{MeV}$
B $24.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$
C $73.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$
D $179\ \mathrm{MeV}$

stemImage.alt: Question 30: The equation → 235 1 121 113 1 U + n Rh + Ag + 2 n 92 0 45 47 0 shows the fission of a uranium−235 nuclide by a slow-moving neutron into a rhodium-121 nuclide,

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert binding energies per nucleon to total energies before finding the difference.
questions.misconception: Binding energies per nucleon can be subtracted directly to get the energy released.

explanation.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Multiply each binding energy per nucleon by the corresponding nucleon number, with zero binding energy for free neutrons. This gives $121(8.26)+113(8.52)-235(7.59)=178.57\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx179\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Uses a much smaller binding-energy gain than the difference between the nuclear totals.
perOption.B: Underestimates the gain by failing to account for the full change in nuclear binding energy.
perOption.C: Undercounts the binding-energy gain of the two daughter nuclei.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The table shows how the count rate from a sample of radioactive nuclide varies with time t. The nuclide has a half life of 50 s. The average background count rate is constant.

t / s

0

50

What count rate will be measured when t = 150 s?
questions.stemText: The table shows how the count rate from a sample of radioactive nuclide varies with time t. The nuclide has a half life of 50 s. The average background count rate is constant. t / s Count rate / Bq 0 72 50 40 What count rate will be measured when t = 150 s? A 8 Bq B 16 Bq C 24 Bq D 32 Bq

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must halve successive drops because the measured rate includes a constant background.
questions.misconception: Applying the half-life to the measured total.

explanation.body: From 0 to 50 s the measured count rate falls by $72-40=32\ \mathrm{Bq}$. Only the source contribution decays, so the drop halves in each successive half-life. From 50 to 100 s it falls by $16\ \mathrm{Bq}$ to $24\ \mathrm{Bq}$, then from 100 to 150 s by $8\ \mathrm{Bq}$ to $16\ \mathrm{Bq}$.

perOption.A: Gives the source contribution at 150 s and omits the background.
perOption.B: Correct. The measured rate is 16 Bq.
perOption.C: Stops at the count rate for 100 s.
perOption.D: Uses the first 50 s drop as the final count rate.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The following diagram shows a radioactive decay chain for thorium-232, which decays through a series of alpha and beta decays to lead (Pb).

What is the number of neutrons for the lead (Pb) nuclide?
questions.stemText: The following diagram shows a radioactive decay chain for thorium-232, which decays through a series of alpha and beta decays to lead (Pb). 훼 훼 훼 훼 Ra Pb Th Rn Po 훽 Ac 훽 Ra 훼 What is the number of neutrons for the lead (Pb) nuclide? A 130 B 134 C 212 D 220

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must track both nucleon and proton numbers through several decays.
questions.misconception: Reading mass number as neutron number.

explanation.body: Along the chain, each alpha decay reduces the mass number by 4 and the proton number by 2, and each beta-minus decay increases the proton number by 1. The final nuclide shown is lead-212 with proton number 82, giving $212-82=130$ neutrons.

perOption.A: Correct. Lead-212 has 130 neutrons.
perOption.B: Gives the neutron number before the last two alpha decays.
perOption.C: Gives the lead mass number instead of its neutron number.
perOption.D: Gives the mass number of the radon intermediate.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Nuclide Y is formed after two successive decays from another nuclide. Each decay can either be an alpha-emission or a beta-emission. Four other nuclides, P, Q, R and S are shown on the diagram.

Which of the nuclides P, Q, R and S is the initial nuclide that, after two successive decays, becomes Y?
questions.stemText: Nuclide Y is formed after two successive decays from another nuclide. Each decay can either be an alpha-emission or a beta-emission. Four other nuclides, P, Q, R and S are shown on the diagram. S R Which of the nuclides P, Q, R and S is the initial nuclide that, after two successive decays, becomes Y? A P B Q C R D S

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Translate the two decay types into grid displacements and identify the parent two steps from Y.
questions.misconception: Changing mass number in beta-minus decay.

explanation.body: An alpha decay moves two squares left and two down, removing two protons and two neutrons. A beta-minus decay moves one square right and one down, changing a neutron into a proton. Working backwards from Y by two beta-minus steps leads to P, so two successive beta-minus decays take P to Y.

perOption.A: Correct. Two beta-minus decays take P to Y.
perOption.B: Q needs one alpha and two beta-minus decays, for three steps.
perOption.C: R has mass number 231, which cannot fall to 228 in changes of zero or four.
perOption.D: S has mass number 235, which cannot fall to 228 in changes of zero or four.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A detector of ionising radiation gives a background count rate of 24 per minute.

A radioactive source is placed close to the detector and the reading is 532 counts per minute. What will be the reading after two half-lives of the source?
questions.stemText: A detector of ionising radiation gives a background count rate of 24 per minute. A radioactive source is placed close to the detector and the reading is 532 counts per minute. What will be the reading after two half-lives of the source? A 127 B 133 C 151 D 157

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Subtract the background before applying two half-lives and restore it to obtain the detector reading.
questions.misconception: Applying radioactive decay to the background count.

explanation.body: Subtract the background first to get the source count rate of $532-24=508$ counts per minute. After two half-lives, the source count rate is $508/4=127$ counts per minute. Adding back the background gives $127+24=151$ counts per minute.

perOption.A: Reports the decayed source count without restoring the background.
perOption.B: Quarters the entire initial detector reading, including the background.
perOption.C: Correct. It includes the source count after decay and the background.
perOption.D: Quarters the total initial reading and then adds the background again.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Antimony-124 undergoes radioactive decay, with a half-life of 60 days, to become tin-124. Tin-124 is stable.

Initially, a sample of antimony-124 contains no tin-124.

For this sample, after what period of time will the ratio $\frac{\text{number of tin-124 nuclei}}{\text{number of antimony-124 nuclei}}$ equals 10?

A between 120 days and 180 days
B 180 days
C between 180 days and 240 days
D 240 days

stemImage.alt: Question 29: Antimony-124 undergoes radioactive decay, with a half-life of 60 days, to become tin-124. Tin-124 is stable. Initially, a sample of antimony-124 contains no tin

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The daughter-to-parent ratio must be converted to a surviving fraction before using the decay law.
questions.misconception: Confusing the daughter-to-parent ratio with the initial-to-remaining ratio.

explanation.body: There are ten tin nuclei for every remaining antimony nucleus, so the surviving fraction is $N/N_0=1/11$. Using $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/60$ per day gives $\ln(1/11)=-(\ln 2/60)t$. Thus $t=208$ days, between 180 and 240 days.

perOption.A: Stops before three half-lives, when the tin-to-antimony ratio is still below 7.
perOption.B: Stops at three half-lives, when the ratio is 7.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio reaches 10 after about 208 days.
perOption.D: Waits four half-lives, by which point the ratio is 15.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Uranium-235 undergoes fission in a reaction shown below, releasing $195\ \mathrm{MeV}$ of energy. The binding energy per nucleon for uranium-235 is $7.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and those for caesium (Cs-143) and rubidium (Rb-90) are approximately $X\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

$\vphantom{U}{}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}+{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\rightarrow{}^{143}_{55}\mathrm{Cs}+{}^{90}_{37}\mathrm{Rb}+3\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$

What is the value of $X$?

A 6.8
B 7.6
C 8.0
D 8.5

stemImage.alt: Question 30: Uranium-235 undergoes fission in a reaction shown below, releasing 195 MeV of energy. The binding energy per nucleon for uranium-235 is 7.6 MeV and those for ca

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert per-nucleon binding energies into totals and account for energy released.
questions.misconception: Counting free neutrons as bound nucleons.

explanation.body: The energy released equals the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235\times7.6$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the sign of the released energy, leading to a decrease in total binding energy.
perOption.B: Carries the uranium binding energy per nucleon over to the products and fails to account for the released energy.
perOption.C: Gives a binding energy increase of only $78\ \mathrm{MeV}$, undercounting the released energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The total binding energy increases by about $195\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
